content.title: Why Balanced Trees and Tries?
content.description: Balanced Trees ensure efficient operations by maintaining tree height, while Tries provide lightning-fast string searching and prefix matching.

content.content: Standard Binary Search Trees can become skewed, causing operations to degrade from O(log n) to O(n). Balanced Trees solve this problem by automatically maintaining near-optimal height. Tries, on the other hand, are specialized tree structures designed for efficient string storage and retrieval.

content.title: Industry Usage
content.content: Balanced Trees power database indexes, operating systems, and file systems, while Tries are widely used in search engines, spell checkers, and autocomplete systems.
Why Do We Need Balanced Trees?
A Binary Search Tree works efficiently only when its height remains small. If nodes are inserted in sorted order, the BST becomes skewed and behaves like a Linked List.
What is a Balanced Tree?

content.definition: A tree where the height remains approximately logarithmic relative to the number of nodes.

content.content: Balanced Trees automatically adjust their structure after insertions and deletions to maintain efficient performance.

content.title: Key Benefit
content.description: Search, insertion, and deletion remain close to O(log n).

content.content: AVL Trees
AVL Trees are self-balancing Binary Search Trees where the height difference between left and right subtrees is at most 1.

content.title: AVL Rule
content.content: Every node must have a balance factor of -1, 0, or +1.
AVL Rotations
When an AVL Tree becomes unbalanced, rotations are performed to restore balance.
Red-Black Trees
Red-Black Trees are self-balancing BSTs that use node colors to maintain approximate balance.

content.definition: A balanced BST where nodes are colored Red or Black and follow special balancing rules.

items.question: Red Node Rule
items.answer: Red nodes cannot have red children.

items.question: Black Height Rule
items.answer: All root-to-leaf paths contain the same number of black nodes.

content.title: Practical Importance
content.content: Many programming language libraries internally use Red-Black Trees because they require fewer rotations than AVL Trees.
AVL vs Red-Black Trees
Introduction to Tries
A Trie (Prefix Tree) is a specialized tree structure used for storing and searching strings efficiently.

content.definition: A tree-like data structure where each node represents a character of a string.

content.title: Prefix Sharing
content.description: Words with common prefixes share the same path, reducing redundant storage.

content.content: Trie Operations

items.question: Insert
items.answer: Add a word character by character.

items.question: Prefix Search
items.answer: Find words sharing a common prefix.

items.question: Delete
items.answer: Remove a word while preserving others.

content.title: What is L?
content.content: L represents the length of the word being searched or inserted.
Autocomplete Using Tries
Autocomplete systems use Tries to quickly retrieve all words beginning with a specific prefix.
Spell Checkers
Spell checkers use Tries to determine whether a word exists and suggest alternatives.

content.title: Daily Usage
content.content: Search bars, IDE code suggestions, and smartphone keyboards heavily rely on Trie-like structures.

content.title: Interview Tip
content.content: If a problem involves prefix matching, autocomplete, dictionaries, or word searches, immediately consider using a Trie.

content.title: Interview Insight
content.description: Balanced Trees guarantee logarithmic performance, while Tries provide highly efficient string operations. Together they form the backbone of many large-scale systems.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: AVL Trees perform rotations to stay balanced.
Both AVL and Red-Black Trees provide O(log n) operations.
Words with common prefixes share paths.
Balanced Trees and Tries solve different classes of problems efficiently.
